content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a prevalent condition in children, often leading to the prescription of antibiotics. A systematic review has shown that the prevalence of AOM in high-income countries is approximately 85.6%. This study is an updated Cochrane Review, originally published in 1997 and subsequently updated multiple times, most recently in 2023. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of antibiotics in children with AOM. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing antibiotics to placebo, as well as immediate antibiotic treatment versus expectant observation (including delayed antibiotic prescribing). The primary outcomes assessed were pain at various time points (24 hours, 2–3 days, 4–7 days, and 10–14 days) and adverse effects likely related to antibiotic use. Secondary outcomes included abnormal tympanometry findings, tympanic membrane perforation, contralateral otitis in unilateral cases, AOM recurrences, serious complications, and long-term effects such as healthcare utilization and parent-reported AOM symptoms. Antibiotics versus Placebo Thirteen trials involving 3,401 children and 3,938 AOM episodes were included, all conducted in high-income countries. The evidence showed that antibiotics do not reduce pain at 24 hours (high-certainty evidence) or at 4–7 days. However, antibiotics reduce pain at 2–3 days by nearly one-third (high-certainty evidence) and at 10–12 days by two-thirds (moderate-certainty evidence). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 20 for pain reduction at 2–3 days and 7 for pain reduction at 10–12 days. Antibiotics were associated with an increased risk of adverse events, such as vomiting, diarrhea, or rash, with a number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome (NNTH) of 14 (high-certainty evidence). Antibiotics also reduced the risk of abnormal tympanometry findings at 2–4 weeks (NNTB 11), slightly reduced the risk of tympanic membrane perforations (NNTB 33), and halved the risk of contralateral otitis episodes (NNTB 11). However, antibiotics did not reduce the risk of abnormal tympanometry findings at 6–8 weeks or 3 months, nor did they reduce the risk of late AOM recurrences. Severe complications were rare, and there was no significant difference in serious complications between children treated with antibiotics and those given a placebo. Immediate Antibiotics versus Expectant Observation Six trials involving 1,556 children from high-income countries were included. Immediate antibiotics may reduce pain at 2–3 days (low-certainty evidence, NNTB 8) but probably do not reduce pain at 3–7 days (moderate-certainty evidence) or at 11–14 days (low-certainty evidence). Immediate antibiotics increased the risk of adverse events such as vomiting, diarrhea, or rash (high-certainty evidence, NNTH 10). They probably do not reduce the proportion of children with abnormal tympanometry findings at 4 weeks, and evidence suggests they may not reduce the risk of tympanic membrane perforation or AOM recurrences. No serious complications were reported in either group. Authors' Conclusions The review indicates that antibiotics likely have no effect on pain at 24 hours, a slight effect on pain in the days following, and only a modest effect on reducing tympanic membrane perforations, contralateral otitis episodes, and abnormal tympanometry findings at 2–4 weeks compared to placebo. In high-income countries, most cases of AOM resolve spontaneously without complications. For every 14 children treated with antibiotics, one child experiences an adverse event (e.g., vomiting, diarrhea, or rash) that would not have occurred if antibiotics were withheld. For most children with mild AOM in high-income countries, an expectant observational approach is appropriate. Clinical management should prioritize adequate pain relief and emphasize the limited role of antibiotics.
